In mathematics, the '''small boundary property''' is a property of certain [[topological dynamics|topological dynamical systems]]. It is dynamical analog of the [[Inductive dimension|inductive definition]] of [[Lebesgue covering dimension]] zero.

== Definition ==

Consider the category of '''topological dynamical system''' (''system'' in short) consisting of a compact metric space <math>X</math> and a homeomorphism <math>T:X\rightarrow X</math>. A set <math>E\subset X</math> is called '''small''' if it has vanishing [[orbit capacity]], i.e., <math>\operatorname{ocap}(E) = 0</math>. This is equivalent to: <math>\forall\mu\in M_{T}(X),\ \mu(E)=0</math> where <math>M_T(X)</math> denotes the collection of <math>T</math>-[[invariant measure]]s on <math>X</math>.

The system <math>(X,T)</math> is said to have the '''small boundary property (SBP)''' if <math>X</math> has a basis of open sets <math> \{O_i\}_{i=1}^\infty </math> whose [[Boundary (topology)|boundaries]] are small, i.e., <math>\operatorname{ocap}(\partial O_i)=0</math> for all <math>i</math>.

== Can one always lower topological entropy?  ==

Small sets were introduced by [[Michael Shub]] and [[Benjamin Weiss]] while investigating the question "can one always lower topological entropy?" Quoting from their article:<ref>Shub, Michael, and B. Weiss. "Can one always lower topological entropy?." Ergodic Theory and Dynamical Systems 11.3 (1991): 535–546.</ref>

"For measure theoretic entropy, it is well known and quite easy to see that a positive entropy transformation always has factors of smaller entropy. Indeed the factor generated by a two-set partition with one of the sets having very small measure will always have small entropy. It is our purpose here to treat the analogous question for topological entropy... We will exclude the trivial factor, where it reduces to one point."

Recall that a system <math>(Y,S)</math> is called a '''factor''' of <math>(X,T)</math>, alternatively <math>(X,T)</math> is called an '''extension''' of <math>(Y,S)</math>, if there exists a continuous surjective mapping <math>\varphi:X\rightarrow Y</math> which is '''eqvuivariant''', i.e. <math>\varphi(Tx)=S\varphi(x)</math> for all <math>x\in X</math>.

Thus Shub and Weiss asked: Given a system <math>(X,T)</math> and <math>\varepsilon>0</math>, can one find a non-trivial factor <math>(Y,S)</math> so that <math>\operatorname{h_{top}}(Y,S)<\varepsilon</math>?

Recall that a system <math>(X,T)</math> is called '''minimal''' if it has no proper non-empty closed <math>T</math>-invariant subsets. It is called '''infinite''' if <math>|X|=\infty</math>.

Lindenstrauss introduced SBP and proved:<ref name=Lin>{{Cite journal|title = Mean dimension, small entropy factors and an embedding theorem|journal = Publications Mathématiques de l'Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques|date = 1999-12-01|issn = 0073-8301|pages = 227–262|volume = 89|issue = 1|doi = 10.1007/BF02698858|first = Elon|last = Lindenstrauss|author-link=Elon Lindenstrauss|url = http://www.numdam.org/item/PMIHES_1999__89__227_0/}}</ref>

'''Theorem:''' Let <math>(X,T)</math> be an extension of an infinite minimal system. The following are equivalent:

# <math>(X,T)</math> has the small-boundary property.
# <math>\operatorname{mdim}(X,T)=0</math>, where <math>\operatorname{mdim}</math> denotes [[mean dimension]].
# For every <math>\varepsilon>0</math>, <math>x\neq y\in X</math>, there exists a factor <math>\varphi_{xy}:(X,T)\rightarrow(Y_{xy},S)</math> so <math>\varphi_{xy}(x) \neq\varphi_{xy}(y)</math> and <math>\operatorname{h_{top}}(Y_{xy},S)<\varepsilon</math>.
# <math>(X,T)=\varprojlim (X_i,T_i)</math> where <math>\{ (X_i, T_i)\}_{i=1}^\infty</math> is an [[inverse limit]] of systems with finite [[topological entropy]] <math>\operatorname{h_{top}}(X_i,T_i)<\infty</math> for all <math>i</math>.

Later this theorem was generalized to the context of several commuting transformations by Gutman, Lindenstrauss and Tsukamoto.<ref>Gutman, Yonatan, Elon Lindenstrauss, and Masaki Tsukamoto. "Mean dimension of <math>\mathbb{Z}^k</math>-actions." Geometric and Functional Analysis 26.3 (2016): 778–817.</ref>

== Systems with no non-trivial finite entropy factors==

Let <math>X=[0,1]^{\mathbb{Z}}</math> and <math>T:X\rightarrow X</math> be the [[shift operator|shift homeomorphism]]
:<math>(\ldots,x_{-2},x_{-1},\mathbf{x_0},x_1,x_2,\ldots)\rightarrow(\ldots,x_{-1},x_{0},\mathbf{x_1},x_2,x_3,\ldots).</math>
This is the [[Baker's map]], formulated as a two-sided shift. It can be shown that <math>(X,T)</math> has no non-trivial finite entropy factors.<ref name=Lin /> One can also find minimal systems with the same property.<ref name=Lin />
